questions.q: Join correctly: 'He was tired. He kept working.'
questions.a: 'He was tired, but he kept working' — contrast logic (expectation vs reality). A wrong answer 'and' misses that keeping-working contradicts the tiredness expectation.

questions.q: Join: 'She was hungry. She ate two sandwiches.'
questions.a: 'She was hungry, so she ate two sandwiches' — cause → result. A wrong answer 'because she ate' reverses causality — the sandwiches didn't cause the hunger.

questions.q: Which is wrong and why: 'I wanted tea, but I drank tea.'
questions.a: The 'but' promises contrast that never arrives — should be 'and'. A wrong answer accepting it shows the student hears 'but' as a pause-word, not a contrast-signal.

questions.q: ______ are joining words — and/but/or join equals, because/so joins reason and result.
Fill in the blank: ______ are joining words — and/but/or join equals, because/so joins reason and result. 'I was tired, SO I slept' — 'so' carries the result.

Fill in the blank: The logic test: read the two ______ — same direction (and), opposite direction (but), choice (or), cause→effect (because/so). 'He studied hard, SO he passed' — cause then result. 'He passed BECAUSE he studied hard' — result then cause.
What is Conjunctions? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Conjunctions are joining words — and/but/or join equals, because/so joins reason and result. 'I was tired, SO I slept' — 'so' carries the result.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Conjunctions?
questions.a: Students default to 'and' for everything, and swap because/so — writing 'He passed, so he studied hard' which reverses cause and effect.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student picks the joiner matching the logic (addition=and, contrast=but, choice=or, reason=because, result=so), combines two sentences with the right conjunction, and spots logic-flips.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The logic test: read the two halves — same direction (and), ______ direction (but), choice (or), cause→effect (because/so). 'He studied hard, SO he passed' — cause then result. 'He passed BECAUSE he studied hard' — result then cause.
